text.p: Officials from 100 countries began week-long talks on Monday to try to get closer to clinching an accord that will oblige signatory states to adopt controls on trade in hazardous chemicals and pesticides, two U.N. agencies said.
The negotiations in Geneva, the third round since March 1996, are to be followed by a session in Brussels in October and a signing ceremony in Rotterdam in December, they added.

The agreement should lead to better global control over industrial and agricultural chemicals that are dangerous to human health or the environment, according to the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Food and Agricultural Organisation (FAO), which are jointly organising the talks.
More than 150 countries take part in two voluntary systems which promote the sharing of information among governments and encourage them to shift towards less hazardous chemicals.
In 1989, the two agencies introduced the "prior informed consent" procedure under which exports of dangerous substances should not proceed unless agreed by the importing country.

"Although the voluntary prior informed consent procedure has been a success, governments now see a need for member countries to adopt mandatory controls on trade in hazardous chemicals and pesticides," UNEP and FAO said in a joint statement.
"Delegates are focussing now on the detailed procedures and the particular chemicals to be included under the agreement."
The chemicals industry has world-wide annual sales of more than $1000 billion, according to the statement.
